evals.prompt: Define eval-driven development for LLM-integrated systems in 2-3 sentences. Include why it is statistical rather than binary.
expected_elements: Evaluations are written before or alongside the LLM system
Eval results gate prompt, model, retrieval, scaffolding, or tooling changes
LLM behavior is stochastic
Pass-rate over a sampled population is the unit of judgment
It is not the same as deterministic unit testing

evals.prompt: Explain the five primitives of eval-driven development and how they work together.
expected_elements: Names eval dataset
Names evaluation function
Names aggregation or pass-rate summary
Names iteration loop
Names regression budget
Explains that the suite stays stable while the system changes

evals.prompt: Distinguish eval-driven-development from agent-eval-design, testing-strategy, evaluation, and error-tracking. Give a mechanism-level reason for each boundary.
expected_elements: agent-eval-design owns construction of task sets, rubrics, graders, and hard negatives
testing-strategy owns deterministic binary software tests
evaluation owns general scoring frameworks and result interpretation
error-tracking owns production incidents or runtime failures
eval-driven-development owns the iterative change-gating discipline

evals.prompt: A teammate says, 'The model passed the prompt unit test once, so we can ship.' Explain the misconception using eval-driven-development.
expected_elements: Rejects one-run pass/fail as sufficient for an LLM system
Explains stochastic outputs require sampled pass-rate
Mentions representative dataset or production-like examples
Mentions aggregation with sample size or confidence/minimum-detectable-change
Mentions regression budget or gate before shipping

evals.prompt: A summarization assistant improves from 82% to 88% on the development eval but drops on a held-out set and human reviewers prefer the old output. Apply eval-driven-development and recommend what to do next.
expected_elements: Identifies possible Goodharting or overfitting to the development eval
Does not treat the 88% headline score as sufficient
Uses held-out set and human calibration as stronger counter-evidence
Recommends diagnosing failures before merging
Mentions refreshing or revising the eval suite or grader
